PT-001: To share my experience, I'm thirty-two years old, and I was initially diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes about five or six years ago, back around 2019. My diagnosis was identified during an annual preventative physical. My routine blood panel showed a fasting glucose of 188 and an A1C of 8.6%. My primary doctor caught it immediately, sat me down without sugarcoating things, and walked me through the reality that my pancreas wasn't keeping up and we had to treat it as Type 2 diabetes. From day one until now, I have managed my diabetes solely with my primary care doctor at our community practice. We check my numbers every six months, though we haven't ever looped in an outside diabetes specialist. In terms of medications over time, we didn't just stay on one pill.  First, the medical team , and then following that they started me on metformin 500mg, which caused some mild stomach cramping before they adjusted me to extended-release 1000mg twice daily, and later on they added glipizide 5mg in the mornings to stimulate insulin secretion when my post-meal readings stayed above 200, and later on they escalated to daily long-acting basal insulin (Lantus) injections in the evening to control overnight fasting surges, and later on they introduced a weekly GLP-1 receptor agonist injection (Ozempic/semaglutide) to curb appetite and improve glycemic control. As of today, my active prescribed regimen is Ozempic weekly pre-filled pen injection together with metformin ER (1000mg daily). Fortunately, accessing the treatment went very smoothly. My doctor handled the paperwork directly, insurance approved tier coverage with a reasonable copay card, and any mild gastrointestinal adjustment subsided within two weeks. Living with this chronic condition day in and day out feels confused by conflicting provider instructions and dosing. At the end of the day, my ultimate hope is avoiding long-term complications like cardiovascular problems, retinopathy, or kidney failure.

To be completely honest, I don't recall the specific names of everything they tried in the past—there was an older pill that gave me diarrhea, and maybe another one for a couple of months, but things got blurry. That's pretty much my story in a nutshell.

That delay was really disheartening because early damage was likely happening while my concerns were being dismissed. Getting to a stable care plan required coordinating across three providers. As of today, my active prescribed regimen is metformin ER (1000mg daily) together with glipizide. Cost and insurance coverage have been a massive stumbling block. When the newer brand-name therapies were brought up, the pharmacy rang up a copay of over $340 a month because my insurance required a prior authorization hurdle that took three weeks to get denied.
